title: Why records matter: cash in your bag is not profit

say: Why records matter: cash in your bag is not profit.
This is the video for Module 1, Why records matter.
A business record is anything written down that shows what happened in your business. A sale, a purchase, money paid out, goods given on credit.
The important thing is that it is written at the time it happens, so you do not need to remember it later.

panel.heading: The written memory of your business
items: A record is written at the time it happens
The head forgets; paper and phones do not
Records help you, your family and lenders

say: Keeping everything in your head works with one product and a few customers. With ten products, credit customers and transfers, the head forgets and remembers the good days more than the bad ones.

say: Your records help you see if you are really making money. They help your family run the shop when you are sick, and they help your cooperative or microfinance bank when you ask for a loan.

say: This is the most important idea in the whole course. Money in your hand is not the same as profit.
For example, Bisi sells fresh pepper and tomatoes in a Lagos market.
By evening she counts about 38,000 naira in her bag. Without a record she thinks, I made 38,000 naira today.
But that morning she bought tomatoes and pepper for about 30,000 naira. And she paid about 2,000 naira for transport and 500 naira for the market ticket. That is 2,500 naira of costs.
So her real profit is about 5,500 naira, not 38,000.
If she spends 10,000 naira on household things tonight, she eats into the money she needs for tomorrow's stock. That is called eating the capital.
There are five records that answer almost every question a small trader has. The sales record shows how much you sold.

panel.heading: Five things to record
items: Sales: what you sold, cash or transfer
Expenses: every cost, even small ones
Stock: goods in, goods out, goods left
Debtors list: who owes you, and when
Cash book: all money in and out

say: And the cash book shows how much money you should have right now.
If five feels like too much, start with sales and expenses. Add the debtors list the very first time someone buys on credit, because credit is where traders lose the most money.

say: Most money leaks out quietly. For example, Amina sells drinks and snacks at a motor park. She loses about 500 naira a day to snacks on credit that are never paid, and things taken by children.

panel.heading: How a 500 naira leak grows
items: About 500 naira a day
x 6 days = 3,000 naira a week
x 52 weeks = 156,000 naira a year
About 26 crates of soft drinks

say: She works 6 days a week. That is 3,000 naira a week.

say: There are about 52 weeks in a year, so that is about 156,000 naira.

say: The best method is the one you will use every day. A notebook is cheap and needs no data. Use a pen, not a pencil. If you make a mistake, draw one line through it. Never tear out pages.

panel.heading: Notebook or phone?
right: Can back up to the cloud
Needs a screen lock and backups

say: A phone adds up for you and can save a copy online. Many traders write in a notebook during the day and type the totals into the phone at night.

say: For example, Kemi sells bread and cannot write easily. She draws a small loaf and a big loaf, and makes one tally mark under the right picture for each sale.

panel.heading: Kemi's picture and tally book
items: A picture for each product
One tally mark for each sale
Credit sales marked in red
Count at night and multiply by the price

say: Credit sales are marked in red.

say: At night she counts 23 small loaves at about 700 naira, and 11 big loaves at about 1,500 naira. Together, about 32,600 naira of bread, with 3,600 naira owed to her.

say: Some people show a fake transfer screen or a fake SMS alert and walk away with goods. Before you release goods, check that the money has entered your own account. Record the transfer only after you confirm it.
If your records are on a phone, set a screen lock, never share your bank PIN or one-time codes with anyone, and back up regularly.

panel.heading: Protect your money and records
items: Confirm transfers in your own account
Do not trust the customer's screen
Set a screen lock on your phone
Never share your PIN or codes
Back up your phone records

say: Now get an exercise book, a biro and a ruler. Set up your first page with three columns: what happened, money in, and money out. A page of honest, untidy numbers is better than a beautiful empty book. Continue with the lessons below.
